Thirty years I have been working this land in Quzhou. I know what this soil likes and what it does not. My husband helps when he can, but he works off-farm most of the year now, so the children too. It is mainly me managing the fields, with hired help at harvest. Seven mu sounds small, but every input I buy comes from real money. I do not waste.

I split my land like this: 5 mu for the wheat-maize rotation, and 2 mu I keep for cotton. Cotton is more work — so much picking — but the price has been okay these past years and I know how to grow it. My neighbors who dropped cotton all regret it a little.

**Wheat (5 mu, planted October):** I use the improved variety — the dealer in town sells Jimai 22 or similar, many around here grow it and get good grain weight. I apply compound fertilizer as base before plowing — about 50 kg of the 15-15-15 compound per mu. Then in spring at jointing I top-dress with urea, about 15 kg per mu. That is my habit. I irrigate three times: before winter, at jointing, and at heading. I cannot skip the heading water — the grain fills badly without it. I spray twice, once for powdery mildew in spring, once for aphids closer to harvest.

**Maize (5 mu, planted June after wheat):** I direct-seed with a small planter — no-tillage right into the wheat stubble. Everyone around me does this now, saves time and diesel. I use Zhengdan 958 most years — familiar seed, reliable yield. I fertilize twice: some compound at sowing and then urea at the big bell stage — that topdressing is the one I never skip. I irrigate twice: once at jointing if it is dry, once when grain is filling. Two pesticide sprays, mainly for corn borer.

**Cotton (2 mu, transplanted late April):** I grow Bt hybrid cotton — bought from the county seed station. Bollworm is no longer the headache it was. My main trouble now is spider mites in July and aphids in May. I plough this plot deep in autumn. Cotton takes more fertilizer than wheat, especially potassium — my dealer told me once that cotton starves for potassium at boll stage and I believe it, I saw the difference. I irrigate more here, four or five times through the summer. Picking is hard work — I hire two day laborers for three days at peak picking.
